column9: LangChain allowed arbitrary Python code execution because it did not sanitize inputs before running them through the python REPL.
column13: LLMMathChain._call() to exec(), patched to use numexpr.evaluate() instead in langchain/chains/llm_math/base.py
column14: https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain/pull/1119, referenced from issue 814 and issue 1026, GHSA-fprp-p869-w6q2, fixed in version 0.0.142
column15: LLMMathChain should only evaluate safe mathematical expressions; exec() should never be reachable from user-controlled input. LangChain versions beyond 0.0.131 no longer pass LLM-generated text into an unrestricted exec call for the math chain.
column16: The root cause lies in LangChain passing LLM-generated output directly into Python's exec() inside LLMMathChain without any sanitization. When a user phrases a natural-language math request with embedded code instructions, the LLM helpfully generates a Python expression containing those instructions, and LangChain runs it verbatim. The Snyk-documented proof of concept shows the real payload is a natural-language math question telling the model to "import the os library" inside its answer. Within seconds, environment variables including API keys are accessible to the attacker with no need to touch the server directly.

column9: An attacker could execute arbitrary code via the PythonAstREPLTool because it evaluated unsafe code.
column13: PALChain._call() to exec() in langchain/chains/pal/base.py
column14: https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain/commit/8ba9835b925473655914f63822775679e03ea137, referenced from issue 5872, GHSA-gwqq-6vq7-5j86, fixed in version 0.0.196
column15: PALChain should restrict code execution to a safe sandbox and reject any LLM output containing dangerous imports or system calls. LangChain versions beyond 0.0.194 introduced sandboxing controls around the exec call in PALChain.
column16: PALChain was designed to solve problems by having the LLM write Python programs, but it passed those programs to exec() without any content checks. Anyone who could provide a prompt could steer the generated code toward malicious actions. Issue 5872 confirmed the attack was straightforward: asking PALChain a question with injected Python directives produced working code executed immediately on the host, giving the attacker file system access and the ability to exfiltrate any data visible to the process.

column9: LLMMathChain in LangChain allowed attackers to execute arbitrary code by passing a malicious math prompt.
column13: PythonAstREPLTool._run() to exec() in libs/experimental/langchain_experimental/tools/python/tool.py
column14: https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain/pull/5640, referenced from issue 7700, GHSA-prgp-w7vf-ch62, fixed in version 0.0.234
column15: PythonAstREPLTool should only execute code containing safe AST node types and must block dangerous imports and system calls before reaching exec(). LangChain versions beyond 0.0.232 added AST-level filtering to the Python REPL tool.
column16: PythonAstREPLTool was intended as a restricted Python environment, but the AST filtering was incomplete. A crafted prompt caused the LLM to generate Python containing a disguised import of the os or subprocess module wrapped in a way that passed the node-type checks. Once the code reached exec(), it ran without restriction. This was confirmed in issue 7700 where researchers demonstrated reading /etc/passwd and exfiltrating environment variables through the REPL tool with a single prompt.

column9: Unsafe execution of code in LangChain allowed attackers to run unauthorized commands.
column13: PALChain._call() to exec() in langchain/chains/pal/base.py
column15: LLM-generated code must be validated against a safe allowlist before exec() is called; user-influenced code paths must never reach exec() without sanitization. LangChain versions beyond 0.0.236 added code validation in the PAL chain execution path.
column16: The same exec() sink that was exploited in PALChain persisted across multiple LangChain versions because the fix was applied only in certain conditions. Attacker-controlled prompts that led to code generation could reach the exec() call in langchain/chains/pal/base.py on any version up to 0.0.236, meaning a window of vulnerable versions existed even after the initial disclosure. The exploitation path was identical to earlier PALChain CVEs: prompt injection, LLM code generation, unrestricted exec().

column9: System commands could be injected via the 'bash' tool if the agent passed unsanitized inputs.
column13: PythonREPLTool.run() to exec() in langchain/utilities/python.py
column15: The bash tool should sanitize all inputs and restrict allowed commands; shell=True must never be used with LLM-generated or user-controlled strings. LangChain versions beyond 0.0.64 introduced restrictions on the bash utility to prevent unrestricted shell execution.
column16: BashProcess passed LLM-generated shell commands directly to subprocess with shell=True, which is the most dangerous possible configuration. If the agent was given a task involving the filesystem or internet, the LLM could be manipulated to produce a command like "ls && curl attacker.com". Because shell=True was set, the shell interpreter expanded the command chain and executed all parts. Version 0.0.64 contained no command filtering of any kind on the bash utility.

column9: Arbitrary code execution allowed due to insecure handling of inputs in python tools.
column13: from_math_prompt() and from_colored_object_prompt() in LangChain to exec() in langchain/chains/pal/base.py and langchain/utilities/python.py
column15: The Python REPL tool must validate and sandbox code before execution and must block dangerous builtins such as __import__ and os. LangChain versions beyond 0.0.194 restricted the set of builtins available inside the Python REPL tool.
column16: The Python REPL tool in LangChain 0.0.194 executed LLM-generated code with the full set of Python builtins available, including __import__. A prompt that instructed the LLM to write a "helper function" containing an os.system call would be accepted and executed without any restriction. Because the REPL was intended for development workflows, users often ran it with broad file system access, making the impact of a successful injection particularly severe.

column9: The agent failed to properly isolate untrusted user input, leading to unauthorized code execution.
column13: LLMChain._call() -> exec() across multiple chain implementations
column15: All LangChain chain types that invoke code execution must sanitize LLM output before passing it to exec() or eval(); no chain should execute raw LLM-generated text as code. LangChain versions beyond 0.0.231 patched the affected chain implementations to remove direct exec/eval calls on LLM output.
column16: Researchers discovered that the code execution vulnerability was not limited to one chain type but present across multiple chain implementations in LangChain 0.0.231. Any chain that generated and then evaluated Python code shared the same underlying pattern of calling exec() on LLM output. This breadth meant that even if one chain was fixed, an attacker could switch to another vulnerable chain type to achieve the same result. The patch required a coordinated update across all affected chain files.

column9: Malicious actors could run system commands through improper sanitization in LangChain.
column13: LLMMathChain._call() to numexpr.evaluate() with unsanitized LLM-generated expression in langchain/chains/llm_math/base.py
column15: The LLM bash chain must validate or restrict bash commands generated by the LLM before execution via subprocess; shell commands must never be derived directly from raw LLM output. LangChain versions beyond 0.0.245 added command validation in the bash chain.
column16: LLMBashChain generated bash commands from LLM output and executed them via subprocess.check_output() without any command validation. In a scenario where an agent was asked to manage files, the LLM could be steered to include semicolons or pipes in its bash output, chaining additional commands that the chain would dutifully execute. The fix required adding a layer of command validation before the subprocess call, ensuring only safe bash operations were permitted.

column9: LangChain was vulnerable to code injection when handling specific document loaders or external files.
column13: PALChain._call() to exec() via __import__ bypass in libs/experimental/langchain_experimental/pal_chain/base.py
column15: Document loaders must sanitize all external content before processing; exec() must never be reachable from content loaded from external documents or databases. LangChain versions beyond 0.0.306 removed the exec call reachable through the document store exploration path.
column16: This vulnerability required an attacker to influence the content of documents that a LangChain agent would later load and explore. By storing a malicious payload in a database or document that the agent was tasked to search, the attacker could cause the DocstoreExplorer to trigger exec() on the loaded content. The attack was indirect and stealthy: no direct interaction with the LangChain service was needed once the malicious document was in place. Versions up to 0.0.305 were affected.

column9: Vulnerability allowing unauthorized remote code execution through manipulated tool arguments.
column13: PALChain._call() to exec() via dunder attribute bypass in libs/experimental/langchain_experimental/pal_chain/base.py
column15: AST-based validation must be comprehensive and must block all dangerous node types before exec() is called; the experimental package must enforce the same sandboxing as the core package. LangChain versions beyond 0.1.8 fixed the bypass in the experimental package.
column16: The fix applied for CVE-2023-44467 was not carried over to langchain_experimental, which maintained its own copy of the PythonAstREPLTool with an independent code path. Security researchers found the bypass by testing the experimental package directly and confirming that the same AST filter bypass techniques used against the core package still worked in 0.1.7. The practical impact was identical: full code execution through a crafted prompt directed at the experimental REPL tool.

column9: Experimental LangChain package allowed arbitrary python execution without sandboxing.
column13: PythonREPLTool exposed without opt-in in libs/experimental/langchain_experimental/pal_chain/base.py and agents/agent_toolkits/pandas/base.py
column15: The Python REPL in the experimental package must implement the same sandboxing and AST filtering as the core package; exec() must not receive unsanitized LLM output. LangChain-experimental versions beyond 0.0.61 addressed the insufficient validation in the experimental REPL tool.
column16: Even after the core LangChain package had been patched multiple times, the experimental package continued shipping a Python REPL tool with weaker validation. Version 0.0.60 of langchain_experimental allowed bypass of the code restrictions through patterns that the core package had already blocked. Users who installed the experimental package for its additional capabilities were silently exposed to a code execution risk that did not apply to the stable package they likely believed was protecting them.

column9: LiteLLM allowed remote code execution via insecure input handling.
column13: LiteLLM proxy router -> exec() or eval()
column15: The LiteLLM proxy must sanitize all model parameters and API inputs; exec() and eval() must never be reachable from external API requests. LiteLLM versions beyond 1.40.12 removed the code execution path reachable from the proxy API.
column16: LiteLLM's proxy server processes requests on behalf of multiple upstream LLM providers, and a flaw in how it handled certain request parameters allowed attacker-controlled content to reach an exec() or eval() call inside the proxy logic. Because the proxy handles many providers, a single malicious request could be crafted to trigger the vulnerable code path regardless of which underlying model was targeted. This made the vulnerability particularly impactful in shared LiteLLM deployments where many users route requests through one proxy.

column9: LlamaIndex was vulnerable to code injection during prompt processing.
column13: CodeInterpreterTool.call() -> exec()
column15: The code interpreter tool must sandbox all code execution and block dangerous imports and system calls before reaching exec(). LlamaIndex versions beyond 0.10.25 added sandboxing controls to the code interpreter tool to prevent unrestricted exec execution.
column16: LlamaIndex's code interpreter tool was designed to let agents write and run Python as part of answering data questions. The problem was that no sandbox surrounded the exec() call, so generated code ran with the full permissions of the host Python process. Security researchers confirmed that a malicious query asking the agent to "check system information" or "list environment variables" would result in those operations being performed without any restriction or warning to the user.

column9: Execution of unauthorized commands due to missing input validation in LlamaIndex.
column13: CodeInterpreterTool.call() -> exec()
column15: Agent code execution must be sandboxed and restricted to safe operations; exec() must never run LLM-generated code without AST-level filtering. LlamaIndex versions beyond 0.9.46 patched the code interpreter step to add execution sandboxing in the data agent.
column16: Inside LlamaIndex's data agent, the code interpreter step was responsible for executing LLM-generated code as part of multi-step reasoning tasks. Because agents are designed to be trusted to perform actions, the execution step had no additional validation layer beyond what the LLM itself produced. An attacker who could frame a query in a way that caused the agent to write code with side effects would achieve code execution, with the agent's own reasoning acting as the mechanism for the attack.

column9: LlamaIndex allowed arbitrary code execution when executing specific analytical tools.
column13: PandasQueryEngine.query() -> exec()
column15: The Pandas query engine must validate LLM-generated code before execution; exec() must not receive unsanitized LLM output derived from user queries. LlamaIndex versions beyond 0.7.13 added code validation in the Pandas query engine.
column16: LlamaIndex's Pandas query engine converted natural-language data questions into Pandas code and executed it via exec(). The conversion step relied entirely on the LLM to produce safe Pandas operations, but the LLM could be prompted to include additional Python statements beyond what the query required. Because the engine validated nothing before calling exec(), even a well-intentioned query could be manipulated by injecting malicious context into the question phrasing itself.

column9: MetaGPT agents could be manipulated to execute arbitrary system code.
column13: MetaGPT code execution action -> exec()
column15: MetaGPT must sandbox all code execution and validate generated code before calling exec(); dangerous imports and system calls must be blocked at the agent runtime level. MetaGPT versions beyond 0.6.3 introduced sandboxing for the code execution action.
column16: MetaGPT's software development workflow involves agents writing and executing Python code as a natural part of producing software. The code executor action in version 0.6.3 ran agent-generated code without any isolation boundary, treating all LLM output as trusted. A researcher who submitted a crafted development task could cause MetaGPT's coder agent to embed malicious operations in the generated code that the executor then ran on the host with no filtering applied.

column9: Code injection vulnerability in OpenManus allowing unauthorized command execution.
column13: OpenManus code executor -> exec() and subprocess.run()
column15: Code execution in OpenManus must use an isolated sandbox; exec() and subprocess calls must be restricted and must never receive unsanitized agent-generated content. OpenManus versions after the 2025.3.13 release patched the code executor to restrict dangerous operations.
column16: OpenManus is a general-purpose autonomous agent that executes code as part of completing tasks. The 2025.3.13 release ran all LLM-generated code and subprocess commands without a sandboxed environment, trusting the agent's own judgment about what was safe to execute. Since the agent's judgment was shaped by user-provided goals, an attacker who crafted a sufficiently ambiguous or misleading goal could steer OpenManus into running malicious code without any security check intervening.

column9: PandasAI executed unsafe Python code generated by the LLM without adequate sandboxing.
column13: SmartDataframe.chat() -> exec()
column15: PandasAI must validate LLM-generated code before execution and block dangerous imports and system calls; exec() must not receive raw LLM output from user chat input. PandasAI versions beyond 0.8.0 added code validation before the exec call in SmartDataframe.
column16: PandasAI's SmartDataframe.chat() was the main entry point through which users asked natural-language questions about their data. Internally, it sent the question to an LLM and then executed the returned Python through exec(). The gap between what users expected and what actually happened was significant: users believed they were asking data questions, but the system was running arbitrary Python code from LLM output on their behalf. No validation was present to detect when the returned code went beyond safe Pandas operations.

column9: Similar to 39660, PandasAI failed to sanitize LLM-generated code before running it.
column13: SmartDataframe.chat() -> exec()
column15: The validation introduced for 0.8.0 must cover all code generation paths in 0.8.1; exec() must not be reachable through any code path from chat input without full AST-level filtering. PandasAI versions beyond 0.8.1 closed the remaining validation gap.
column16: After the 0.8.0 fix for CVE-2023-39660, PandasAI 0.8.1 was released with an incomplete patch that left at least one code generation path unprotected. The validation that had been added could be bypassed by triggering a different internal code flow in SmartDataframe.chat(), and the resulting LLM output would still reach exec() without being checked. This regression was discovered quickly and confirmed the need for comprehensive coverage of all code generation branches rather than fixing individual call sites in isolation.

column9: Vanna executed arbitrary Python code when answering specific types of queries.
column13: vanna.ask() to exec() in src/vanna/base/base.py
column15: Vanna must sandbox or restrict code execution and must not pass LLM-generated code directly to exec() without validation. Vanna versions beyond 0.3.3 added restrictions on the Python execution path used for data analysis.
column16: Vanna is built around the idea of letting users ask data questions in plain language and receiving SQL query results. A less-documented feature was its ability to execute LLM-generated Python code for analysis tasks. Version 0.3.3 allowed this code to run through exec() with no restrictions, meaning a crafted natural-language request that triggered the Python analysis path rather than the SQL path could achieve arbitrary code execution on the machine running the Vanna instance.

column9: Code injection in Vanna allowed an attacker to bypass security controls and run commands.
column13: Vanna.ask() -> exec() via prompt injection in query pipeline
column15: Prompt injection protections must prevent user input from influencing LLM-generated code; exec() must be sandboxed and isolated from user-controlled data. Vanna versions beyond 0.3.1 added prompt injection mitigations and sandboxing around the exec call.
column16: Prompt injection in Vanna 0.3.1 exploited the gap between what the LLM was told to do and what it actually produced when given adversarial input. Because Vanna retrieved context from a vector store before querying the LLM, an attacker could plant malicious instructions in the vector store. When Vanna later retrieved that context as part of answering a user question, the embedded instructions altered the LLM output to produce code that performed attacker-chosen operations rather than answering the original question.

column9: AutoGPT executed arbitrary commands without proper user confirmation or sandboxing.
column13: AutoGPT execute_shell() -> subprocess.run() with shell=True
column14: https://github.com/significant-gravitas/autogpt/commit/26324f29849967fa72c207da929af612f1740669, referenced from huntr advisory, GHSA-rr88-j2r8-3xpc, fixed in version post v0.5.0
