AutoGPT versions after commit 26324f2 patched the shell execution command to prevent OS command injection.
column16: AutoGPT v0.5.0 included a shell execution command as one of its built-in agent capabilities. The command passed user-defined or LLM-selected shell instructions to subprocess.run() with shell=True, which meant the shell interpreter received the full command string and expanded any operators like &&, |, or ;. The huntr.com advisory documented the exploit path: an attacker crafted a goal that led the agent to select the shell execution command and supply malicious arguments, achieving OS-level code execution without any validation step.

column9: Code injection vulnerability in Langchain.
column13: LangChain tool executor -> exec()
column15: All code execution tools must enforce comprehensive AST-based validation before exec() is called; exec() must never receive raw LLM output from any tool execution path. LangChain versions beyond 0.3.51 tightened the code execution path in the Python tool.
column16: In LangChain 0.3.51, researchers identified that a code execution path in the Python tool remained reachable through a combination of prompt techniques that bypassed the existing AST validation. The vulnerability demonstrated a recurring pattern in the LangChain codebase: fixes applied to specific call sites were sometimes bypassed when attackers found alternate routes to the same exec() sink. Each bypass required a new patch, confirming that exec() should never be reachable from LLM output regardless of how many validation layers are present.

column9: Code injection vulnerability in smolagents.
column13: LocalPythonExecutor.evaluate_call() to exec() via __str__/__repr__ dunder bypass in src/smolagents/local_python_executor.py (lines 61, 910-917)
column15: smolagents CodeAgent must use an isolated sandbox with restricted builtins and must block os and subprocess access before calling exec() on any LLM-generated code. smolagents versions beyond 1.25.0.dev0 introduced LocalPythonInterpreter sandboxing for the CodeAgent.
column16: smolagents was specifically designed for code-based agents where the LLM writes and executes Python to complete tasks. Version 1.25.0.dev0 ran all agent-generated code through exec() in the standard Python environment without restriction, as sandboxing had not yet been implemented. The CodeAgent class treated every piece of LLM-generated code as implicitly trusted, which meant that a user who provided a goal with adversarial framing could cause the agent to produce and execute malicious Python before any human review.

column9: Code injection vulnerability via the LlamaIndex CLI.
column13: LlamaIndex CLI code tool -> exec()
column15: The CLI code execution tool must validate and sandbox all LLM-generated code before exec() is called; CLI-invoked code generation must not produce executable output without restriction. LlamaIndex CLI versions beyond 0.12.20 added sandboxing to the CLI code execution pathway.
column16: The LlamaIndex CLI tool included a code generation command that invoked the LLM to produce Python scripts, then executed those scripts through exec() as part of the CLI workflow. Because CLI tools are typically run with developer-level permissions, the absence of any sandbox around the exec() call meant that a malicious or manipulated code generation request could execute with those elevated permissions. This was a particular concern in automated pipeline environments where the CLI was invoked non-interactively.

column9: Code injection vulnerability in SuperAGI allowing arbitrary execution.
column13: SuperAGI code writing tool -> exec() and subprocess.run()
column15: SuperAGI code execution must run in an isolated environment; exec() and subprocess calls must be restricted and must never execute unsanitized agent-generated code. SuperAGI versions after v0.0.14 patched the code writing tool to use sandboxed execution.
column16: SuperAGI v0.0.14 included a code writing tool that generated Python files as part of agent task completion. The generated files were executed immediately through exec() and subprocess as part of the same action, with no review step or sandboxing between generation and execution. An attacker who crafted a task description with embedded malicious intent could cause the code writing tool to produce and execute harmful code, all within the normal flow of the agent completing what appeared to be a legitimate task.

column9: Code injection in Anthropic Git MCP server allowing command execution via git.
column13: Anthropic Git MCP server -> subprocess.run() for git operations
column15: The Git MCP server must sanitize all repository parameters before passing them to subprocess; subprocess must never receive unsanitized user or agent input. Anthropic Git MCP server versions after 2025.12.18 patched the git handler to sanitize argument inputs.
column16: The Anthropic Git MCP server handled git operations by constructing commands from input parameters and passing them to subprocess. Before the December 2025 patch, repository URLs and git arguments were not sanitized before subprocess received them. An attacker who could control what repository URL or git option the server processed could inject shell metacharacters that expanded into additional commands when subprocess executed the git operation, achieving OS command execution on the MCP server host.

column9: Code injection vulnerability in MetaGPT.
column13: MetaGPT code execution action -> exec() and subprocess
column14: https://github.com/geekan/MetaGPT/security/advisories, fixed in version post affected release
column15: MetaGPT must sandbox all agent-generated code execution; dangerous imports and subprocess calls must be blocked before exec() is called in the execution action. MetaGPT versions beyond the affected release patched the code executor to use an isolated execution environment.
column16: MetaGPT's code execution action ran agent-generated Python without an isolation boundary in this affected version. The multi-agent development workflow produced code at the end of several reasoning steps, and by the time exec() was called the output was treated as trusted internal data rather than as potentially adversarial LLM output. Security research showed that injecting malicious intent into early stages of the task description could propagate through the agent reasoning chain and produce harmful code that the executor would run unsandboxed.

column9: Code injection vulnerability in MetaGPT prior to 0.8.1.
column13: MetaGPT code execution action -> exec()
column15: MetaGPT must use a sandboxed execution environment for all agent-generated code; exec() must not receive unsanitized LLM output from any agent action. MetaGPT versions beyond 0.8.1 introduced a sandboxed code execution environment for agent actions.
column16: MetaGPT versions before 0.8.1 executed agent-generated code through exec() in the standard Python environment. The vulnerability mirrored earlier MetaGPT CVEs and highlighted that sandboxing had not yet been systematically applied across all code execution paths in the framework. A user who submitted a software development task with adversarial framing could cause MetaGPT's coder agent to include harmful operations in the generated code, which the executor would then run without restriction on the host.

column9: Code injection in Cybersecurity AI.
column13: CAI agent executor -> exec() and subprocess.run()
column14: https://github.com/aliasrobotics/cai/commit/09ccb6e0baccf56c40e6cb429c698750843a999c, fixed in version post affected release
column15: CAI must execute all agent-generated code in a sandboxed environment; dangerous system calls and subprocess access must be blocked from LLM-generated code. Affected CAI versions were patched to restrict code execution to an isolated runtime.
column16: The Cybersecurity AI (CAI) agent was built for security research tasks and included code execution capabilities as part of its analysis workflow. The commit at 09ccb6e patched a path where agent-generated code and subprocess commands were executed without isolation during the autonomous analysis loop. Because CAI targets security research use cases, the absence of sandboxing was particularly notable: an attacker who could influence CAI's task input could cause it to execute offensive security tools or harvest credentials from the host.

column9: Code injection vulnerability in Langflow's CSV Agent node.
column13: Langflow CSV Agent node -> exec()
column15: The CSV Agent node must sandbox all code execution and must never pass LLM-generated code to exec() without AST-level filtering. Langflow versions beyond 1.8.0 patched the CSV Agent node to use sandboxed code execution.
column16: Langflow's CSV Agent node converted natural-language data analysis requests into Python code for processing CSV files, then ran that code through exec(). The node was designed for non-technical users who would not expect their data questions to result in arbitrary code execution, and no sandboxing was present before Langflow 1.8.0. By crafting a CSV file with embedded trigger content, an attacker could cause the LLM to generate malicious Python during the analysis step that then executed on the Langflow server.

column9: Template engine injection in Langchain allowed attackers to execute code via crafted templates.
column13: LangChain PromptTemplate.format() -> jinja2.Environment.from_string() with user input as template
column15: Prompt templates must use jinja2.sandbox.SandboxedEnvironment for all rendering; user input must never be used as the template string itself, only as a variable value. LangChain versions beyond 0.3.80 replaced the unsafe Jinja2 environment with a sandboxed renderer.
column16: This was a Jinja2 server-side template injection in LangChain's prompt template system. When user-supplied input was used as the template string itself rather than as a variable within a template, the Jinja2 engine would interpret any Jinja2 directives embedded in the input. A payload using config.__class__.__init__.__globals__ could extract the Flask or Python runtime environment. Because LangChain applications commonly accept user-defined prompts, this attack was reachable in a wide range of deployments using Jinja2 template syntax.

column9: SQL injection vulnerability in LangChain allowed attackers to modify backend databases.
column13: SQLDatabaseChain._call() -> cursor.execute() with concatenated user input
column15: SQL queries must use parameterized statements; user input must never be concatenated directly into SQL strings before cursor.execute() is called. LangChain versions beyond 0.0.247 switched the SQL database chain to parameterized queries.
column16: LangChain's SQL database chain allowed agents to answer natural-language questions by converting them to SQL queries. The chain assembled queries by concatenating user input into SQL strings before passing them to cursor.execute(), creating a textbook SQL injection condition. An attacker who prompted the agent with a carefully formed question containing SQL syntax could break out of the intended query structure and perform unauthorized operations including data extraction, table modification, or deletion on the connected database.

column9: SQL Injection in LangChain via improper sanitization of user prompts translated to SQL.
column13: SQLDatabaseChain._call() -> cursor.execute() with unsanitized LLM-generated SQL
column15: The SQL chain must use parameterized queries for all database interactions; LLM-generated SQL must be validated before being passed to cursor.execute(). LangChain versions beyond 0.2.5 patched the SQL database chain to prevent injection through LLM-generated queries.
column16: In LangChain 0.2.5, the SQL database chain executed LLM-generated SQL queries without parameterization. The LLM was responsible for generating safe SQL from the user's natural-language question, but nothing prevented a crafted prompt from causing the LLM to generate malicious SQL that included operations beyond what the user intended to request. Researchers confirmed that prompts containing SQL keywords in natural language could influence the generated query to include UNION-based data extraction or destructive clauses.

column9: SQL Injection in LlamaIndex when querying structured data stores.
column13: NLSQLTableQueryEngine.query() -> cursor.execute()
column15: The SQL query engine must parameterize all queries; LLM-generated SQL must be validated before cursor.execute() is called with any user-derived content. LlamaIndex versions beyond 0.11.23 added parameterized query enforcement in the natural language SQL query engine.
column16: LlamaIndex's NLSQLTableQueryEngine translates natural-language questions into SQL and executes them. In version 0.11.23, the generated SQL was passed directly to cursor.execute() without parameterization. A natural-language question embedding SQL injection syntax survived the LLM translation in a form that the database driver interpreted as a second query or a manipulation of the query structure. This class of vulnerability is difficult to detect because the injection exists in natural language before translation, not in the SQL itself.

column9: SQL Injection vulnerability in LlamaIndex due to unescaped user inputs in SQL generation.
column13: NLSQLTableQueryEngine.query() -> cursor.execute()
column15: All SQL execution must use parameterized queries; LLM output must not be directly concatenated into SQL strings before cursor.execute() is called. LlamaIndex versions beyond 0.9.28.post2 enforced parameterized queries in the structured store SQL query engine.
column16: The LlamaIndex SQL query engine in 0.9.28.post2 converted user queries to SQL and executed them via cursor.execute() using string concatenation. Because the LLM cannot reliably sanitize SQL at the query generation stage, any user who understood the query format could craft input that would produce injected SQL clauses. The advisory documents confirmed that UNION SELECT payloads embedded in natural language caused the engine to execute multi-statement queries returning data from tables outside the intended scope.

column9: SQL injection in Vanna allowed unauthorized access to the underlying database.
column13: Vanna.ask() -> cursor.execute() with LLM-generated SQL
column15: Vanna must validate and parameterize all SQL before execution; dangerous SQL operations such as DROP and DELETE must be blocked from LLM-generated output. Vanna versions beyond 0.3.4 added SQL validation and operation restrictions before cursor.execute().
column16: Vanna 0.3.4's database connector executed LLM-generated SQL through cursor.execute() without parameterization or operation filtering. A user who discovered that the query engine would sometimes return a different result format for certain question types could craft input that steered the LLM toward generating DROP or DELETE statements. The advisory for GHSA-3698-9476-gg98 confirmed that Vanna would execute these destructive operations against the configured database without any confirmation step or restriction.

column9: Another SQL injection vulnerability in Vanna 0.3.4.
column13: Vanna.ask() -> cursor.execute() without operation restrictions
column15: SQL generation must be restricted to SELECT statements only; all queries must be parameterized before cursor.execute() is called. Vanna versions beyond 0.3.4 patched the SQL connector to enforce read-only query generation.
column16: This SQL injection in Vanna 0.3.4 specifically targeted the database connector layer, where LLM-generated SQL was executed without restricting the type of SQL operations permitted. An attacker who found that their natural-language queries were translated into INSERT or UPDATE statements under certain conditions could exploit the absence of an operation allowlist to perform write operations on the connected database, going beyond the read-only data analysis workflow Vanna was designed to support.

column9: Vanna 0.6.2 was susceptible to SQL injection via crafted prompts.
column13: Vanna.ask() -> cursor.execute() with unvalidated LLM SQL output
column15: Vanna must enforce read-only SQL execution and parameterize all queries; LLM-generated SQL must be validated against an allowlist of safe operations before cursor.execute() is called. Vanna versions beyond 0.6.2 patched the database connector to restrict and parameterize all SQL execution.
column16: Vanna 0.6.2 continued to pass LLM-generated SQL to cursor.execute() without enforcing read-only constraints or parameterized queries. The GHSA-g7hm-f83q-jhr6 advisory documents how a user query phrased to ask about database structure or statistics could cause the LLM to generate SQL that exposed schema details or manipulated records. Because Vanna was commonly deployed connected to production databases for business intelligence, the impact of unauthorized write operations or data extraction was significant.

column9: SQL injection vulnerability in LlamaIndex structured query components.
column13: NLSQLTableQueryEngine.query() -> cursor.execute()
column15: The SQL query engine must use parameterized queries for all database interactions; LLM-generated SQL must be validated before cursor.execute() is called in all affected versions. LlamaIndex versions beyond 0.12.27 closed the parameterization gap in the SQL query engine.
column16: A regression in LlamaIndex versions 0.12.21 through 0.12.27 reintroduced a SQL injection condition in the NLSQLTableQueryEngine. Versions before and after this range were not affected, making this a targeted window of vulnerable releases. The advisory GHSA-f9c3-2wr4-r3hh confirmed that the parameterization that had been implemented in earlier versions was accidentally removed during a refactor, and LLM-generated SQL was once again concatenated directly into query strings before cursor.execute() was called.

column9: SQL Injection in LangGraph SQLite checkpointing allowed modification of state.
column13: SqliteSaver.put() -> cursor.execute() with unsanitized checkpoint key
column15: The SQLite checkpointer must use parameterized queries for all checkpoint read and write operations; checkpoint keys must never be concatenated into SQL strings. LangGraph checkpoint SQLite versions beyond 3.0.1 switched all checkpoint queries to parameterized statements.
column16: The LangGraph SQLite checkpointer stored and retrieved agent state using checkpoint keys that were incorporated into SQL queries through string concatenation. An attacker who could control checkpoint identifiers, either directly or through an agent workflow, could inject SQL into the checkpoint key and manipulate the SQLite database storing the agent's state. This could result in reading checkpoint data belonging to other sessions or corrupting the state store that LangGraph agents depend on for multi-step task continuity.

column9: SuperAGI allowed path traversal and arbitrary file read/write operations.
column13: SuperAGI file tool -> open() without path validation
column15: File tools must validate and normalize all paths; os.path.abspath() output must be checked against the allowed base directory before any file operation is performed. SuperAGI versions after v0.0.14 added path validation to the file system tools.
column16: SuperAGI's file system tools performed read and write operations on paths derived from agent task descriptions and LLM output. The huntr advisory documented how an attacker could frame a task that directed the agent to read or write a file using a path containing ../ sequences. Because no base directory enforcement was applied, the agent obligingly accessed the requested path, allowing traversal to arbitrary locations on the host including configuration files, SSH keys, and environment variable files.

column9: Devika was vulnerable to path traversal allowing agents to read sensitive files.
column13: Devika researcher agent -> open() without base directory restriction
column14: https://github.com/stitionai/devika/security/advisories/GHSA-xpwp-v4hv-6j93, GHSA-xpwp-v4hv-6j93, fixed in version post advisory
column15: The file reader must validate all paths against the allowed project directory; path traversal sequences such as ../ must be detected and blocked before open() is called. Devika patched the researcher agent to restrict file reads to the project root.
column16: Devika's researcher agent built for autonomous software development included a file reading capability that accepted paths from the agent's internal reasoning about what files to examine. Since those paths ultimately derived from user-provided project context, an attacker could name a file or directory using traversal sequences. The GHSA-xpwp-v4hv-6j93 advisory confirmed that Devika would follow the traversal path and return the contents of files well outside the intended project directory.

column9: Devika allowed arbitrary file writing via path traversal.
column13: Devika coder agent -> open() in write mode without path restriction
column14: https://github.com/stitionai/devika/security/advisories/GHSA-8w3c-mxwj-6jcv, GHSA-8w3c-mxwj-6jcv, fixed in version post advisory
column15: The file writer must restrict all write operations to the project directory; paths must be normalized using os.path.realpath() and checked against the project root before open() is called in write mode. Devika patched the coder agent to enforce write path restrictions.
column16: Devika's coder agent wrote generated code to disk as part of its software development workflow. The file path for each output file was determined by the agent's understanding of the project structure, which in turn was derived from user-supplied project descriptions. An attacker who specified a project that referenced files using ../ path sequences could cause Devika to write generated files outside the intended project directory, overwriting host files such as startup scripts or shell configuration files.

column9: Devika path traversal vulnerability allowing unauthorized file access.
column13: Devika project manager -> open() and file system operations without base directory enforcement
column14: https://github.com/stitionai/devika/security/advisories/GHSA-9hg8-m8rj-7gxv, GHSA-9hg8-m8rj-7gxv, fixed in version post advisory
column15: All file operations must validate paths against the project root using os.path.realpath(); directory traversal sequences must be detected and blocked across all file management tools. Devika patched the project manager to enforce a base directory boundary on all file system operations.
column16: Multiple file management operations in Devika's project manager were affected by the same absence of base directory enforcement. The GHSA-9hg8-m8rj-7gxv advisory covered file reads, writes, and directory listings that all accepted paths without resolving or validating them against the project root. The breadth of affected operations meant that even after patching individual functions, a comprehensive fix required adding os.path.realpath() validation to the entire file management layer.

column9: Path traversal in Langchain-chatchat allowed reading arbitrary files.
column13: LangChain-Chatchat file handler -> open() with unsanitized upload path
column15: The file handler must normalize and validate all file paths before open() is called; all file operations must be restricted to the designated upload directory. LangChain-Chatchat patched the file handler to enforce path sanitization on all uploaded file paths.
column16: LangChain-Chatchat allowed users to upload files as context for their conversations. The file handler stored uploaded files at paths derived from user-supplied filenames without sanitizing the path component. An attacker who uploaded a file with a filename like ../../config/settings.py would cause the handler to write the file at that traversal path on the server. Because Chatchat ran with application-level permissions, this enabled overwriting server configuration or code files through the ordinary file upload interface.

column9: Path Traversal vulnerability in LangChain.
column13: LangChain document loader -> open() with user-supplied file path
column15: Document loaders must validate all file paths and restrict access to files within allowed directories; user-supplied paths must be resolved and checked against a base directory before open() is called. LangChain patched the affected document loader to enforce path boundary checks.
column16: A LangChain document loader accepted file paths from user input or agent tool calls and opened those files without validating that they were within an allowed directory. In agent workflows where file analysis was a tool the agent could invoke, an attacker could craft a goal that caused the agent to call the document loader with a traversal path, reading sensitive host files as part of what appeared to be a normal document analysis task.

column9: Quivr was vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), allowing agents to access internal networks.
column13: Quivr web fetcher tool -> requests.get() with unvalidated URL
column15: The web fetcher must validate all URLs and block requests to internal and private IP ranges including 127.0.0.1, 10.x.x.x, and 192.168.x.x before calling requests.get(). Quivr versions beyond 0.0.236 added SSRF protection with URL allowlisting to the web fetcher tool.
column16: Quivr's web fetcher tool made HTTP requests on behalf of the agent to URLs that were partially or fully user-controlled. Because no SSRF protection was implemented, the tool would happily fetch http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ on AWS-hosted instances, returning cloud instance metadata including IAM role credentials. The GHSA-j6j2-3j6p-cx7m advisory confirmed that internal network addresses and cloud metadata endpoints were reachable through the web fetcher with no additional configuration required.

column9: Serialization injection allowed code execution or data tampering when loading configurations.
column13: LangChain URL document loader -> requests.get() with user-supplied URL
column15: URL loaders must validate all destination URLs and block requests to internal network addresses; SSRF protection must be applied before requests.get() is called. LangChain patched the URL loader to add SSRF protections including internal IP blocklisting.
column16: LangChain's URL-based document loader accepted arbitrary URLs and fetched them using requests.get() without any destination filtering. An agent that used document loading as part of its research workflow could be directed to load a document from an internal IP address, effectively making the LangChain host perform the request on the attacker's behalf. This is the classic SSRF pattern: using a trusted server's network access to reach resources that the attacker cannot access directly from outside.

column9: Serialization injection in langchain_core allowed execution via unsafe deserialization.
column13: langchain_core deserializer -> pickle.loads() and yaml.load() on untrusted data
column15: Deserialization must use safe methods exclusively; pickle.loads() must not be used with untrusted data and yaml.safe_load() must replace yaml.load() for all untrusted input. LangChain-core versions beyond 1.2.5 replaced unsafe deserialization calls with safe alternatives.
column16: LangChain-core used pickle.loads() and yaml.load() to deserialize objects that could originate from user-provided data. Pickle deserialization in Python is well-known to execute arbitrary code during the deserialization process itself, making any application that pickles user-controlled data fundamentally vulnerable to code execution regardless of any subsequent validation. An attacker who could provide a malicious serialized LangChain object would achieve code execution the moment deserialize() was called on it, with no further interaction required.

column9: Vulnerability in an AI agent orchestration platform.
column13: AI agent orchestration platform executor -> exec() or privileged API endpoint
column14: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-67117, no GitHub advisory available, see NVD references for details
column15: The agent platform must validate all execution requests and enforce access controls; exec() and privileged API endpoints must never be reachable from untrusted agent input. The affected platform was patched to enforce request validation and restrict code execution paths.
column16: This vulnerability in an AI agent orchestration platform allowed a crafted agent request to reach a privileged code execution or API pathway without triggering the expected authorization checks. The NVD entry does not identify the specific repository, making independent verification difficult, but the vulnerability class matches a common pattern in agent orchestration systems where the complexity of routing logic creates gaps between what the authorization layer checks and what the execution layer permits.

column9: Shell Injection in Langflow CI pipeline.
column13: Langflow pipeline handler -> code injection via unsanitized configuration
column14: https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/security/advisories/GHSA-87cc-65ph-2j4w, GHSA-87cc-65ph-2j4w, fixed in version post advisory
column15: Pipeline configuration must be fully validated; untrusted input must never influence pipeline execution logic or trigger code execution. Langflow patched the pipeline handler to sanitize all configuration inputs before execution.
column16: Langflow's CI/CD pipeline component processed flow deployment configurations supplied by users. A maliciously crafted pipeline configuration contained fields that the pipeline handler evaluated without sanitization, causing the execution engine to run attacker-controlled code as part of the deployment process. Because pipeline execution ran with the permissions needed to deploy Langflow components, the impact included not just code execution but potential modification of the Langflow deployment itself.

column9: OS Command Injection in MetaGPT.
column13: MetaGPT shell tool -> os.system() and subprocess.run()
column15: The shell tool must sanitize all command inputs and must never pass unsanitized agent or user input to os.system() or subprocess; dangerous command patterns must be detected and blocked. MetaGPT patched the shell tool to add command sanitization.
column16: MetaGPT's shell tool executed OS commands as part of its software development agent workflow. The tool received commands derived from agent reasoning and LLM output and passed them to os.system() without sanitization. Because MetaGPT operated in development environments where shell access is expected, the shell tool was readily available to agent steps. An attacker who crafted a task causing MetaGPT to reach the shell tool with malicious command arguments would achieve OS-level code execution on the development host.

column9: SSRF vulnerability in AutoGPT.
column13: AutoGPT web browsing command -> requests.get() with unvalidated URL
column15: The web tool must validate all URLs and block requests to private IP ranges before requests.get() is called; internal addresses must be enumerated and blocked. AutoGPT patched the web requests command to add SSRF URL validation.
column16: AutoGPT's web browsing command fetched URLs using requests.get() and returned the page content to the agent for further processing. Because no URL validation was applied, the command would fetch any URL the agent was directed to, including internal network addresses. An attacker who crafted a goal that led the agent to browse to a private IP range could use AutoGPT as a proxy to probe the internal network, retrieve cloud metadata credentials, or interact with internal administrative interfaces.

column9: SSRF vulnerability in AutoGPT.
column13: AutoGPT web request handler -> requests.get() with unvalidated URL
column15: All HTTP request functions in AutoGPT web tools must validate destination URLs against an SSRF blocklist; no web request may target internal network addresses. AutoGPT patched the related SSRF path as a companion fix to CVE-2025-62615.
column16: This SSRF vulnerability in AutoGPT represented a separate but related web request path that the CVE-2025-62615 fix did not cover. Researchers found that after the first patch was applied, a second code path in the web request handling layer remained unprotected and could be reached through a different sequence of agent actions. Together CVE-2025-62615 and CVE-2025-62616 illustrate that SSRF protection must be applied comprehensively at every HTTP request call site, not just the most obvious one.

column9: SSRF vulnerability in CrewAI.
column13: CrewAI web tool -> requests.get() and httpx.get() with unvalidated URL
column15: CrewAI web tools must validate all URLs and block requests to private and loopback addresses before making HTTP requests; SSRF protection must cover both requests and httpx HTTP libraries. CrewAI patched the web tools to add URL validation with SSRF blocklisting.
column16: CrewAI's web browsing tool enabled agents to fetch URLs as part of research tasks. The tool accepted URLs from agent reasoning output and passed them to requests.get() or httpx.get() without validating against an SSRF blocklist. A task that directed the CrewAI research agent to gather information from a specific URL could be crafted to point at internal network resources, allowing an attacker to leverage the agent's web tool to access services behind the firewall that would otherwise be unreachable from the external network.

column9: Auth bypass in ServiceNow Virtual Agent.
column13: ServiceNow Virtual Agent SSO handler -> authentication bypass
column14: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mwg5-cwh8-88m5, GHSA-mwg5-cwh8-88m5, fixed in patched ServiceNow release
column15: The SSO handler must validate all authentication assertions and must block bypass attempts via manipulated SSO tokens or responses; every protected endpoint must require valid authentication. ServiceNow patched the Virtual Agent SSO handler to close the authentication bypass.
column16: The ServiceNow Virtual Agent SSO handler processed authentication assertions as part of its single sign-on integration. A flaw in how the handler validated SSO tokens allowed a specially crafted authentication assertion to pass validation without containing valid credential data. The GHSA-mwg5-cwh8-88m5 advisory documented how an attacker with knowledge of the assertion format could authenticate to the Virtual Agent API without possessing valid SSO credentials, gaining access to agent configuration and conversation data.

column9: Code Injection / RCE in Langflow.
column13: Langflow executor -> exec() and subprocess via unsanitized flow configuration
column15: The Langflow executor must validate all flow configurations and restrict dangerous operations; exec() and subprocess must not be reachable through attacker-controlled flow definitions. Langflow versions beyond 1.9.0 patched the executor to validate and restrict flow execution.
column16: Langflow's flow executor processed flow definitions that could contain code-executing nodes configured by users. In versions before 1.9.0, the executor did not validate node configurations before executing them, allowing a malicious flow definition containing a crafted code node to execute attacker-controlled code on the Langflow server. Because Langflow is often self-hosted and users have full control over flow definitions, this vulnerability could be exploited by any user with access to the flow builder.

column9: Command Injection in GitHub Copilot.
column13: GitHub Copilot command executor -> subprocess.run() with unsanitized input
column14: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3m2x-p87c-pwv6, GHSA-3m2x-p87c-pwv6, fixed in patched Copilot release
column15: Command execution must sanitize all inputs and must never use shell=True with user or LLM-controlled strings; all suggested commands must be validated before subprocess is called. GitHub Copilot patched the command executor to add input sanitization.
column16: The GHSA-3m2x-p87c-pwv6 advisory documents a command injection vulnerability in GitHub Copilot's execution runner. Copilot suggested code and commands in developer contexts where those suggestions were sometimes executed automatically by the runner without additional sanitization. An attacker who could influence the context presented to Copilot, for example through malicious code in an open file or repository, could steer Copilot to suggest a command containing injection payloads that the runner would execute on the developer's machine.

column9: Command Injection in Claude Code.
column13: Claude Code executor -> subprocess.run() and exec()
column14: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/security/advisories/GHSA-x56v-x2h6-7j34, GHSA-x56v-x2h6-7j34, fixed in patched Claude Code release
column15: Claude Code must execute all generated code in a sandboxed environment; dangerous system calls and subprocess access must be restricted from agent-generated code. Claude Code was patched to add sandboxing controls to the code execution runner.
column16: Claude Code's execution runner ran agent-generated code and shell commands as part of its coding assistant workflow. The GHSA-x56v-x2h6-7j34 advisory confirms a path where code execution occurred without sandboxing, meaning that a crafted coding task could cause Claude Code to produce and execute malicious code on the developer's machine. Given that Claude Code operates with the developer's own file system permissions, a successful exploit had direct access to all files and credentials accessible to the developer's user account.

column9: Vulnerability in Metagpt AI Agent Framework.
column13: MetaGPT code execution action -> exec() and subprocess
column15: MetaGPT must use a sandboxed execution environment for all agent-generated code; dangerous operations must be restricted from LLM-generated code before exec() is called. MetaGPT patched the execute code action to enforce sandboxed execution.
column16: In this MetaGPT release, the code execution action passed agent-generated Python to exec() without any isolation layer. The vulnerability followed the same pattern as earlier MetaGPT CVEs: a multi-agent development workflow produced code that the executor treated as trusted internal output rather than potentially adversarial LLM content. Injecting malicious intent into the initial task description could propagate through multiple reasoning steps and ultimately cause the executor to run harmful code on the host.

column9: Vulnerability in Fastgpt AI Agent Framework.
column13: FastGPT workflow executor -> exec() and HTTP request handlers
column15: FastGPT must validate all workflow node configurations and restrict code execution and HTTP requests to safe operations; attacker-controlled workflow definitions must never reach exec() or unchecked HTTP clients. FastGPT patched the workflow executor to add node validation.
column16: FastGPT's workflow executor processed visual flow definitions that users created through the FastGPT interface. Flow nodes could include code execution or HTTP request components, and the executor processed these node configurations without validating that their parameters were safe. A malicious workflow node configuration could cause the executor to run arbitrary code or make HTTP requests to internal network addresses, with the workflow execution layer providing the mechanism for the attack.

column9: SSRF in modelscope agentscope.
column13: AgentScope web tool -> requests.get() with unvalidated URL
column15: AgentScope web tools must block requests to internal and private IP ranges; URL validation must be enforced before any HTTP request is made by the agent. AgentScope patched the web tools to add SSRF URL validation.
column16: AgentScope's web tool enabled agents to fetch URLs as part of web-based tasks. The tool passed URLs derived from agent reasoning and task descriptions to requests.get() without URL validation. Because AgentScope agents operate in tool-use loops where the LLM selects which tool to call and with what arguments, an attacker who influenced the task description could steer the agent to invoke the web tool with an internal network URL, reaching resources behind the deployment firewall from outside.

column9: SSRF in modelscope agentscope.
column13: AgentScope web tool -> requests.get() through secondary request path
column15: All HTTP request paths in AgentScope must implement SSRF protection and URL validation; the SSRF blocklist must cover every function that makes outbound HTTP requests. AgentScope patched the companion SSRF path as part of the same fix cycle as CVE-2026-6606.
column16: Following the discovery of CVE-2026-6606, researchers identified a second SSRF-vulnerable HTTP request path in AgentScope that was not covered by the initial fix. This second path was reached through a different sequence of agent tool invocations and also lacked URL validation. The existence of two separate SSRF paths in the same codebase reinforced that SSRF protection must be treated as a framework-level concern applied consistently, not as an individual fix applied to a single function.

column9: Code Injection in modelscope agentscope.
column13: AgentScope code execution service -> exec() and subprocess
column15: AgentScope code execution must use an isolated sandbox; dangerous functions must be blocked from LLM-generated code before exec() or subprocess is called. AgentScope patched the code execution service to enforce sandboxed execution for agent-generated code.
column16: AgentScope's code execution service ran agent-generated Python and subprocess commands without a sandboxed environment. The service was part of AgentScope's tool infrastructure and was invoked when agents decided to execute code as part of their reasoning loop. Because agents are autonomous and their tool selections are driven by the task they are given, a crafted task could guide the agent to invoke the code execution service with malicious code that would then run unsandboxed on the AgentScope host.

column9: Incorrect Authorization in MCP agents.
column13: MCP agents authorization middleware -> authorization bypass
column14: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pqp2-x3gp-9g37, GHSA-pqp2-x3gp-9g37, fixed in patched MCP agents release
column15: The authorization middleware must validate agent permissions for every action and must block privilege escalation via malformed or unexpected requests; no action must be reachable without a valid permission check. MCP agents patched the middleware to enforce comprehensive authorization.
column16: The GHSA-pqp2-x3gp-9g37 advisory documents incorrect authorization in the MCP agents middleware layer. The middleware was responsible for checking that agents only performed actions within their defined permission scope, but a flaw in the permission validation logic allowed agents to craft requests that bypassed the scope check. This enabled an agent with limited permissions to access or trigger operations reserved for higher-privileged agents, potentially escalating what actions could be performed through the MCP agent ecosystem.

column9: Code Injection in MetaGPT.
column13: MetaGPT code execution action -> exec() and subprocess
column15: MetaGPT must isolate all code execution in a sandbox and restrict dangerous imports and system calls from agent-generated code. MetaGPT versions beyond the affected release patched the code executor with sandboxing.
column16: MetaGPT before the patched version executed agent-generated code without sandboxing as part of its autonomous software development pipeline. This was one of several code execution CVEs affecting MetaGPT over multiple release cycles, reflecting a recurring challenge in frameworks that rely on LLM-generated code execution as a core feature. Each discovered CVE in the MetaGPT execution path highlighted that exec() without sandboxing is untenable in any production agentic system.

column9: SSRF in LangChain.
column13: LangChain HTTP request tool -> requests.get() with user-controlled URL
column15: The HTTP tool must validate all URLs against an SSRF blocklist and block requests to internal IP ranges; SSRF protection must be applied before requests.get() is called. LangChain versions beyond 1.1.14 added SSRF protections to the HTTP request tool.
column16: LangChain's HTTP request tool accepted URLs from agent reasoning and user input and fetched them without applying any SSRF blocklist. In agent workflows where HTTP access was a routine tool call, an attacker could craft a prompt that caused the agent to invoke the request tool with a private IP address or cloud metadata URL. Because the request was made from the LangChain host rather than the attacker's machine, internal services that were not exposed externally were reachable through the agent.

column9: SSRF in LangChain text splitters.
column13: LangChain text splitter remote loader -> requests.get() with unvalidated URL
column15: Text splitters must validate all URLs before fetching remote content; SSRF protections must be applied to prevent requests to internal network addresses. LangChain versions beyond 1.1.2 added URL validation to the text splitter remote content loading path.
column16: LangChain's text splitter included a code path that fetched remote content from URLs to split into chunks. This URL-based content loading path did not validate the destination URL against an SSRF blocklist, meaning that a text splitting request pointing to an internal URL would cause the LangChain host to make the outbound request. The vulnerability was less obvious than direct HTTP tool SSRF because it appeared in text processing infrastructure rather than an explicitly network-oriented tool.

column9: SSRF in PraisonAIAgents.
column13: PraisonAIAgents web tool -> requests.get() with unvalidated URL
column14: https://github.com/MervinPraison/PraisonAI/security/advisories/GHSA-8f4v-xfm9-3244, GHSA-8f4v-xfm9-3244, fixed in version post advisory
column15: The web tool must implement URL allowlisting or blocklisting; internal network addresses must be blocked before requests.get() is called. PraisonAIAgents patched the web tools to add SSRF URL validation.
column16: PraisonAIAgents included web browsing tools that enabled agents to retrieve content from URLs during task execution. The web tools passed agent-selected URLs to requests.get() without validating against internal network ranges. In deployment environments where PraisonAI ran on cloud infrastructure, this created a path to cloud metadata credentials: an agent directed to research a topic could be steered to browse http://169.254.169.254/ and return the metadata response as part of its research findings.

column9: Prompt Injection in LangChain.
column13: LangChain prompt handler -> jinja2.Environment.from_string() with unsanitized user input
column15: User input must be sanitized and treated as data before inclusion in prompts; prompt templates must enforce strict separation between instructions and user content. LangChain versions beyond 0.3.84 and 1.2.28 added prompt injection mitigations to the prompt handler.
column16: This prompt injection vulnerability in LangChain arose when user-supplied text was incorporated into prompts without being treated as data. Instead of escaping or sandboxing user content, the prompt handler placed raw user input into positions in the prompt template where it would be read by the LLM as instructions. An attacker who understood the prompt structure could craft input that overrode the system instructions, causing the LLM to ignore its intended behavior and perform attacker-directed actions instead.

column9: Code Injection in PraisonAI.
column13: PraisonAI code agent -> exec() and subprocess
column15: PraisonAI code execution must use a sandboxed environment; exec() and subprocess must not be accessible from LLM-generated code without restriction. PraisonAI patched the code agent to add execution sandboxing.
column16: PraisonAI's code agent generated and executed Python as part of its autonomous reasoning loop. The agent ran code in the standard Python environment without restriction, trusting that the code it produced would align with the task intent. Because task intent was shaped by user input, a crafted task could cause PraisonAI to generate code with intentionally harmful side effects that the code agent would then execute, achieving arbitrary code execution through the agent's own programming capability.

column9: Argument Injection in mcp-server-kubernetes.
column13: mcp-server-kubernetes kubectl runner -> subprocess.run() with unsanitized arguments
column15: All kubectl commands must be constructed from validated parameters only; subprocess must not receive user-controlled strings directly and shell injection via argument manipulation must be prevented. The MCP server for Kubernetes was patched to sanitize all kubectl argument inputs.
column16: The MCP server for Kubernetes constructed kubectl commands by assembling parameters received from agent tool calls. Before the patch, Kubernetes resource names, namespace values, and label selectors passed to the MCP server were incorporated into kubectl command strings without sanitization. By supplying a resource name containing shell metacharacters or additional kubectl flags, an attacker could inject arguments that caused the kubectl invocation to perform operations beyond what was intended by the original tool call.

column9: Path Traversal in OpenClaw.
column13: OpenClaw file tool -> open() without path boundary enforcement
column14: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/security/advisories/GHSA-hr5v-j9h9-xjhg, GHSA-hr5v-j9h9-xjhg, fixed in version post advisory
column15: The file handler must validate and normalize all file paths; directory traversal sequences must be detected and blocked before open() is called. OpenClaw patched the file tool to add path boundary enforcement.
column16: OpenClaw's file handling tool performed file operations at paths derived from agent task descriptions and LLM output. The GHSA-hr5v-j9h9-xjhg advisory confirmed that path validation was absent, allowing an attacker to frame a task that caused OpenClaw to read a file at a traversal path outside the intended directory. The tool would process the traversal path literally and return file contents from arbitrary host locations including system files and credentials.

column9: Symlink Traversal in OpenClaw.
column13: OpenClaw file tool -> os.symlink() and open() without symlink resolution
column14: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/security/advisories/GHSA-7xr2-q9vf-x4r5, GHSA-7xr2-q9vf-x4r5, fixed in version post advisory
column15: The file tool must resolve all symlinks using os.path.realpath() and validate the resolved path against the allowed base directory before performing any file operation. OpenClaw patched the file tool to add symlink resolution and base directory validation.
column16: The GHSA-7xr2-q9vf-x4r5 advisory for OpenClaw documents a symlink traversal vulnerability where the file tool followed symbolic links without checking whether the resolved path remained inside the allowed directory. An attacker who could create a symlink in a directory accessible to OpenClaw could cause the tool to follow that link and access files at the symlink's destination, bypassing any directory boundary that would otherwise prevent access to those files.

column9: Auth Bypass in PraisonAI.
column13: PraisonAI auth handler -> authentication bypass
column15: The auth handler must enforce authentication for all protected routes and must block bypass attempts via manipulated or malformed tokens; every protected API endpoint must require a valid authentication check. PraisonAI patched the auth handler to close the authentication bypass.
column16: PraisonAI's auth handler contained a logic flaw in how it validated authentication tokens for protected API routes. An attacker who crafted a request with a manipulated token format that the validator accepted as valid despite containing no legitimate credential data could gain unauthorized access to PraisonAI's agent management APIs. This would allow the attacker to create, modify, or read agent configurations and conversation data without possessing a valid account.

column9: Code Injection in Langflow.
column13: Langflow code runner component -> exec()
column15: Langflow code execution must use a sandboxed environment; exec() must not receive unsanitized input from user-created flow components. Langflow patched the code runner component to enforce sandboxed execution.
column16: Langflow's code runner component executed user-defined Python code nodes that were part of flow definitions. Before the patch, the code runner called exec() on node code without sandboxing, trusting that the code was safe because it came from the user's own flow. In multi-user Langflow deployments, a malicious user could create a flow containing a code node with harmful Python that would execute on the Langflow server when the flow was run, affecting the entire shared deployment.

column9: Code Injection in PinchTab.
column13: PinchTab execution runner -> exec() and subprocess
column15: PinchTab must sandbox all code execution; exec() and subprocess must not receive agent-generated content without restriction and sandboxing. PinchTab patched the execution runner to add code sandboxing.
column16: The commit at 25b3374 in the PinchTab repository patched a code injection vulnerability in the execution runner where agent-generated code was passed to exec() without sandboxing. PinchTab's agent performed browser-based tasks and included a code execution capability for automation. A crafted task directed at the code execution feature could cause the agent to generate and run malicious Python on the PinchTab host, with the agent's automation purpose masking the malicious intent of the task.

column9: SSRF in PinchTab.
column13: PinchTab web tool -> requests.get() with unvalidated URL
column15: The web fetcher must validate all URLs and block requests to internal IP ranges before requests.get() is called. PinchTab patched the web fetcher to add SSRF URL validation.
column16: The commit at c824574 in PinchTab patched an SSRF vulnerability in the web fetcher tool. PinchTab's agent browsing capability fetched URLs without validating against internal network ranges. Because PinchTab automated browser-like tasks on behalf of users, an attacker could craft a task that directed PinchTab to retrieve content from internal network resources, making the PinchTab server act as an unwitting proxy into the private network.

column9: SSRF in PinchTab.
column13: PinchTab HTTP client -> requests.get() and httpx.get() with unvalidated URL
column14: https://github.com/pinchtab/pinchtab/security/advisories/GHSA-qwxp-6qf9-wr4m, GHSA-qwxp-6qf9-wr4m, fixed in version post advisory
column15: The HTTP client must enforce an SSRF blocklist; requests to private IP ranges must be rejected before any outbound HTTP request is made. PinchTab patched the HTTP client to add SSRF protection.
column16: The GHSA-qwxp-6qf9-wr4m advisory documents an SSRF vulnerability in PinchTab's HTTP client tool. PinchTab used this client to make programmatic HTTP requests as part of its automation workflow. The client accepted target URLs from agent instructions without applying SSRF filtering, enabling an attacker to direct PinchTab to make requests to internal services that were accessible from the PinchTab host but not from external networks.

column9: Auth Bypass in Langflow.
column13: Langflow login API -> authentication bypass
column15: The auth module must enforce authentication for all protected endpoints; token validation must not be bypassable through malformed or empty credentials. Langflow patched the auth module to close the authentication bypass in the login API.
column16: Langflow's login API endpoint contained an authentication bypass where the token validation logic failed to reject certain malformed credential combinations. An attacker who discovered the bypass could authenticate to the Langflow API without valid credentials, gaining access to all flow management functions including viewing, creating, and executing flows. In shared Langflow deployments this exposed other users' flow configurations and the ability to run arbitrary flows as an authenticated user.

column9: Cypher Injection in Graphiti.
column13: Graphiti search handler -> Cypher cursor.execute() with concatenated user input
column15: Cypher queries must use parameterized statements; user input must never be concatenated into Cypher query strings before execution. Graphiti versions beyond 0.28.2 added parameterized query enforcement to the search handler.
column16: Graphiti used Neo4j as its graph database backend and constructed Cypher queries using string concatenation with user-provided search terms. Because Cypher injection follows the same pattern as SQL injection, an attacker could embed Cypher query operators in a search input to break out of the intended query structure and access graph nodes outside the intended scope. The advisory for GHSA-related Graphiti confirms that parameterized Cypher queries were absent in versions up to 0.28.2.

column9: Symlink Traversal in OpenClaw.
column13: OpenClaw filesystem handler -> os.symlink() and open() without symlink resolution
column15: OpenClaw must resolve all symlinks using os.path.realpath() and validate the resolved path against the base directory before any file operation; symlinks pointing outside the base directory must be rejected. OpenClaw patched the filesystem handler to add symlink resolution.
column16: The commit at 125f407 in the OpenClaw repository addressed a symlink traversal vulnerability in the filesystem handler. An attacker who placed a symlink in a location accessible to OpenClaw could cause file operations to follow the link to its destination outside the intended directory boundary. Because os.path.realpath() was not called before validating paths, the pre-resolution path appeared safe while the post-resolution target was outside the allowed area.

column9: Auth Bypass in Coral Server.
column13: Coral Server auth endpoint -> authentication bypass
column14: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-30970, no GitHub advisory available, see NVD references for details
column15: Auth endpoints must validate credentials for all protected routes; bypass via missing or malformed tokens must be prevented at every endpoint. Coral Server patched the auth endpoints to enforce authentication on all protected routes.
column16: Coral Server's auth endpoint failed to enforce authentication on protected API routes in this release. The specific flaw in the endpoint validation logic allowed requests with missing or malformed authentication tokens to bypass the credential check and receive authorized responses. An attacker who discovered the bypass could access Coral Server functionality without an account, with the extent of impact depending on which protected operations were reachable through the unprotected endpoint.

column9: Auth Bypass in Coral Server.
column13: Coral Server auth middleware -> authentication bypass
column14: https://github.com/Coral-Protocol/coral-server/security/advisories/GHSA-ccx7-7wv9-c55x, GHSA-ccx7-7wv9-c55x, fixed in version post advisory
column15: Auth middleware must be consistently applied to all protected routes; token validation must be enforced for every request and must not be skippable through routing tricks. Coral Server patched the auth middleware to prevent authentication bypass.
column16: The GHSA-ccx7-7wv9-c55x advisory documents an authentication bypass in Coral Server's middleware layer. Unlike endpoint-level bypasses, middleware bypasses affect every route that relies on the middleware for authentication. Coral Server's auth middleware could be bypassed through specific routing patterns or request structures that caused the middleware to skip its validation step, allowing unauthenticated requests to flow through to protected handlers without triggering any auth check.

column9: Auth Bypass in Coral Server.
column13: Coral Server auth validator -> authentication bypass
column14: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-30968, no GitHub advisory available, see NVD references for details
column15: The auth validator must correctly enforce all authentication requirements and must handle all edge cases in token validation without allowing bypass. Coral Server patched the auth validator to close the credential validation logic flaw.
column16: Coral Server's auth validator contained a logic flaw that allowed certain credential combinations to pass validation despite not representing valid authentication state. The specific bypass condition documented in the NVD entry involved a token handling edge case that the validator did not cover. An attacker who discovered this edge case could construct a request that satisfied the validator's check without possessing a legitimately issued credential, gaining unauthorized access to Coral Server.

column9: SSRF in PinchTab.
column13: PinchTab browser tool -> requests.get() with unvalidated URL
column14: https://github.com/pinchtab/pinchtab/security/advisories/GHSA-rw8p-c6hf-q3pg, GHSA-rw8p-c6hf-q3pg, fixed in version post advisory
column15: The browser tool must validate all URLs and block requests to loopback and private network addresses before making any HTTP request. PinchTab patched the browser tool to add SSRF URL validation.
column16: The GHSA-rw8p-c6hf-q3pg advisory documents SSRF in PinchTab's browser automation tool. PinchTab's browser tool was designed to navigate web pages as part of automation workflows, and it accepted target URLs from the task definition without filtering for internal addresses. An attacker could task PinchTab with browsing to an internal URL, causing the PinchTab host to make the request and return the response through the browser tool, reaching services protected by network perimeter controls.

column9: Remote Code Execution in AutoGPT.
column13: AutoGPT command executor -> exec() and subprocess
column15: AutoGPT must sandbox all code execution; subprocess and exec() must not receive unsanitized agent-generated or user-controlled content. AutoGPT patched the command executor to add sandboxed execution for agent-generated code.
column16: AutoGPT's command executor ran agent-generated code and subprocess commands without isolation in this affected version. This CVE represents a continuation of the same vulnerability class found in CVE-2024-1881, indicating that the sandboxing improvements applied after earlier disclosures were incomplete. A new task crafted to reach the code execution path would result in LLM-generated code running on the AutoGPT host with full host permissions, following the same agent-directed code execution pattern as the earlier CVE.

column9: SSRF in LangChain.
column13: LangChain HTTP request tool -> requests.get() with attacker-controlled URL
column15: All HTTP request tools must validate destination URLs against an SSRF blocklist covering all private IP ranges; SSRF protection must be applied before requests.get() is called. LangChain versions beyond 1.2.11 added SSRF protection to the request tool.
column16: LangChain's HTTP request tool in versions up to 1.2.11 accepted URLs from agent reasoning and external input without SSRF filtering. An attacker who could influence a LangChain agent's task could direct it to invoke the request tool against internal network addresses. Because LangChain is often deployed on cloud infrastructure, this created a reliable path to retrieve cloud instance metadata credentials by directing the agent to fetch the metadata endpoint URL.

column9: Denial of Service in AutoGPT.
column13: AutoGPT memory handler -> uncontrolled resource consumption
column15: AutoGPT must implement resource limits on all memory operations; agent tasks must have enforced timeouts and resource consumption caps to prevent denial of service. AutoGPT patched the memory handler to add resource limits and task timeouts.
column16: A denial of service condition in AutoGPT was triggered by tasks that caused the memory handler to perform unbounded operations. An attacker who crafted a goal designed to maximize memory usage, for example by asking AutoGPT to build an ever-expanding knowledge base or perform recursive memory operations, could exhaust system resources and cause the AutoGPT instance to become unresponsive. The commit at 57a06f70 in the AutoGPT repository patched the memory handler to enforce operational limits.

column9: Arbitrary File Write in Semantic Kernel.
column13: Semantic Kernel file IO plugin -> open() in write mode without path restriction
column15: The file plugin must restrict all write operations to allowed directories; path normalization using os.path.realpath() must be applied and validated against the base directory before open() is called in write mode. Semantic Kernel patched the file IO plugin to enforce path restrictions.
column16: Semantic Kernel's file IO plugin performed write operations to paths provided by agent instructions without validating that those paths remained within an allowed directory. In Semantic Kernel deployments where agents had access to the file plugin, a task that directed the agent to save output to a specific path could be crafted to use a traversal sequence, causing the plugin to overwrite files outside the intended directory. The impact depended on what files were accessible to the process running the Semantic Kernel agent.

column9: SSRF in LibreChat.
column13: LibreChat web fetcher service -> requests.get() with unvalidated URL
column15: The web fetcher must validate and restrict all URLs; internal IP ranges and localhost must be blocked before any HTTP request is made. LibreChat patched the web fetcher service to add SSRF URL validation.
column16: LibreChat's web fetcher service made HTTP requests on behalf of agents and users during conversation workflows. The service did not validate destination URLs against an SSRF blocklist before calling the HTTP client, meaning that agent-directed or user-supplied URLs pointing to internal resources would be fetched and returned as part of the conversation. This enabled an attacker to retrieve the contents of internal services through LibreChat's server by embedding internal URLs in agent tasks or direct web fetch requests.

column9: Auth Bypass in LibreChat.
column13: LibreChat auth middleware -> authentication bypass
column15: The auth middleware must enforce authentication on all protected routes consistently; token validation must not be bypassed through request manipulation. LibreChat patched the auth middleware to close the authentication bypass.
column16: LibreChat's authentication middleware contained a logic flaw that allowed certain request patterns to bypass the token validation step. Because this was a middleware-level bypass rather than an endpoint-level one, it affected all protected routes that depended on the middleware for authentication. An attacker who discovered the bypass condition could access user session data and agent APIs without valid credentials, potentially impersonating other users or accessing their conversation history.

column9: Insecure File Upload in LibreChat.
column13: LibreChat file upload handler -> open() and fs.writeFile() without path validation
column15: The file upload handler must validate file paths and extensions; all uploaded files must be stored in an isolated upload directory and path traversal sequences must be blocked. LibreChat patched the file handler to enforce upload directory restrictions.
column16: LibreChat's file upload service stored uploaded files using paths derived from user-supplied filenames processed by fs.writeFile() without sanitizing the path component. An attacker who uploaded a file with a filename containing ../ sequences could cause the service to write the file at a traversal path on the LibreChat server, overwriting arbitrary files. Because LibreChat ran with server-level permissions, this enabled overwriting application code, configuration files, or other sensitive server data.

column9: Path Traversal in Langflow.
column13: Langflow file reader component -> open() with user-supplied file path
column14: https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/security/advisories/GHSA-f43r-cc68-gpx4, GHSA-f43r-cc68-gpx4, fixed in version post advisory
column15: The file reader must normalize and validate all paths; only files within allowed project directories should be accessible and path traversal sequences must be blocked before open() is called. Langflow patched the file reader component to enforce path boundary checks.
column16: The GHSA-f43r-cc68-gpx4 advisory documents path traversal in Langflow's file reader component. The component accepted file paths from the Langflow UI flow configuration without applying base directory validation. A user who created a Langflow flow with a file reader node pointing to a traversal path could cause the component to read arbitrary files from the Langflow server filesystem and return their contents as part of the flow output.

column9: SSRF in Langflow.
column13: Langflow URL fetcher component -> requests.get() with unvalidated URL
column15: The URL fetcher must implement an SSRF blocklist; requests to private IP ranges must be blocked before requests.get() is called. Langflow patched the URL fetcher component to add SSRF URL validation.
column16: Langflow's URL fetcher component fetched remote content as part of flow execution, accepting URLs from the flow configuration without SSRF filtering. In multi-user Langflow deployments, a user who built a flow with a URL fetcher node pointing to an internal network address could cause the Langflow server to make requests to internal resources on their behalf. This enabled access to internal services protected by network controls that would otherwise be inaccessible to the external user.

column9: XSS in DeepChat.
column13: DeepChat message component -> innerHTML with unsanitized message content
column15: DeepChat must sanitize all user-provided content before rendering; innerHTML must never receive unsanitized data and a Content-Security-Policy must prevent inline script execution. DeepChat patched the message component to add HTML sanitization before rendering.
column16: DeepChat's message rendering component inserted user message content into the DOM using innerHTML without first sanitizing it. A user who sent a message containing an HTML script tag or an event handler attribute would cause the tag to be rendered and the script to execute in the receiving browser session. This classic XSS pattern was particularly damaging in a chat application because it could silently steal session tokens from other users viewing the same conversation, enabling account takeover without any visible indication of an attack.

column9: SQL Injection in Neuron.
column13: Neuron API handler -> cursor.execute() with concatenated query parameters
column15: The Neuron API must use parameterized queries for all database operations; user input must never be concatenated into SQL strings before cursor.execute() is called. Neuron versions beyond 2.8.11 switched the API query handler to parameterized statements.
column16: The commit at 44bab85d in the neuron-core repository patched a SQL injection in Neuron's API query handler. API query parameters were assembled into SQL strings through concatenation before being passed to cursor.execute(), creating a direct injection path. An attacker who sent API requests with crafted parameter values could manipulate the query structure to extract data from tables they were not authorized to access or perform write operations through the read-oriented API.

column9: Read-Only Bypass in Neuron.
column13: Neuron access control -> authorization bypass (read-only restriction not enforced)
column15: Access control must enforce read-only restrictions on all write endpoints; the privilege check must cover every operation type and must not be bypassable through request manipulation. Neuron versions beyond 2.8.11 fixed the access control logic to enforce read-only restrictions consistently.
column16: The commit at 72735d0e in the neuron-core repository patched a read-only access bypass in Neuron's access control layer. The access control logic that was supposed to restrict read-only users from performing write operations contained an edge case where a specific request pattern satisfied the read-only check despite attempting a write operation. An attacker with a read-only account who discovered this pattern could perform unauthorized modifications to Neuron's data through what appeared to the system to be valid read requests.

column9: Command Injection in MCP Server Kubernetes.
column13: MCP Server Kubernetes kubectl runner -> subprocess.run() with unsanitized parameters
column15: All kubectl commands must be constructed from validated, enumerated parameters only; shell injection via argument manipulation must be prevented and subprocess must not receive user-controlled strings directly. The MCP Server for Kubernetes was patched to enforce kubectl argument sanitization.
column16: The commit at d091107f in the MCP Server Kubernetes repository patched a command injection vulnerability in the kubectl runner. The runner assembled kubectl commands by concatenating user-supplied resource identifiers such as deployment names, namespace values, and label selectors directly into the command string. An attacker who supplied a resource name containing shell metacharacters or additional kubectl subcommands could cause the MCP server to execute kubectl operations beyond what was intended, potentially affecting Kubernetes cluster resources outside the intended scope.

column9: XSS in AI Playground OAuth.
column13: AI Playground OAuth callback page -> innerHTML with unsanitized OAuth callback parameters
column15: The OAuth callback must sanitize all URL parameters before rendering; a Content-Security-Policy must prevent script execution and OAuth state parameters must be validated. The AI Playground OAuth handler was patched to sanitize callback parameters before DOM insertion.
column16: The commit at 3f490d04 in the Cloudflare agents repository patched an XSS vulnerability in the AI Playground OAuth callback page. The callback page received OAuth redirect parameters and rendered them directly into innerHTML to display status information to the user. An attacker who crafted a malicious OAuth redirect URL with a script payload in the callback parameters could cause a victim to load the callback page and execute the attacker's JavaScript in their browser session, enabling session token theft or account takeover.
